title: Sounds, Greetings & Respect
mission: Pronounce essential sounds and open and close a culturally appropriate greeting.
can_do: I can greet someone appropriately and reproduce essential sound patterns.

beats.text: Welcome to Lesson 1: Sounds, Greetings & Respect.
In this lesson, you'll learn how to greet one person or a group, ask how someone is, answer politely, and close the conversation well.
Listen first. Then we'll practise the expressions together and use them in a short conversation.
Let's begin with the sounds you'll hear in today's greetings.
isiZulu vowels are pure and steady: a, e, i, o, u. They don't glide the way many English vowels do, so keep each one clean.
isiZulu also has click sounds. You'll see them written with the letters c, q and x. You'll meet them in real words as the course goes on — for now, just listen for them.
Today, focus on clear vowels and a relaxed, even rhythm.
Sound examples from the pronunciation guide: model each slowly, then naturally. Learner repeats after each one.
Now let's greet someone.
Here are the key expressions for this lesson.
Listen to each one first. I'll say it slowly, then at a natural speed — and then it's your turn.

beats.en: I’m fine, and how are you?
Thank you, I am fine. Stay well.

beats.text: Good. Now let's build on that with a few more expressions you'll use in the same situations.

beats.en: Good day, how are you all?
We are well, and how are you all?

beats.text: Let's sharpen your pronunciation.
I'll say each one slowly, then the way you'd hear it in a real conversation. Listen to the rhythm, then try it yourself.

beats.en: I’m fine, and how are you?
Thank you, I am fine. Stay well.

beats.text: LIVE EXAMPLE SLOT — explain one sound or rhythm feature you hear as a native speaker. Keep it practical. Any new isiZulu wording must be flagged for language QA before the final cut.
Now let's use these in a real exchange.
I'll perform the whole conversation once. Then we'll take it turn by turn — you'll play one part, and then we'll switch.
Perform the exchange naturally once. Then take it turn by turn: the learner plays one role, then switches roles.

beats.en: I’m fine, and how are you?
beats.speaker: Speaker B

beats.en: Thank you, I am fine. Stay well.
beats.speaker: Speaker A

beats.en: Good day, how are you all?
beats.speaker: Speaker A

beats.en: We are well, and how are you all?
beats.speaker: Speaker B

beats.text: Time to check what you remember.
I'll give you the English. Try to say it in isiZulu before I give you the answer.
How do you say “Hello, how are you?”
Pause 4 sec — let the learner answer before you reveal.
How do you say “I’m fine, and how are you?”
Pause 4 sec — let the learner answer before you reveal.

beats.en: I’m fine, and how are you?

beats.text: How do you say “Thank you, I am fine”?
Pause 4 sec — let the learner answer before you reveal.
How do you say “Thank you, I am fine. Stay well”?
Pause 4 sec — let the learner answer before you reveal.

beats.en: Thank you, I am fine. Stay well.

beats.text: How do you say “Hello” to one person?
Pause 4 sec — let the learner answer before you reveal.
Feedback: acknowledge the meaning first, then model the exact source form and ask for one clean repeat.
Let's put it all together in a short role-play.
Picture this: you arrive at a friend's home and greet the family — first one person, then everyone together. Ask how they are, answer when they ask you, and close the conversation politely.

Set the scene without giving a full answer script. The learner uses at least three approved forms. Change one detail or ask one follow-up so the learner retrieves rather than recites. If they're stuck, give the English meaning as a cue before showing the target form. Don't rescue too early.
Support bank — show only if the learner is stuck:

beats.en: I’m fine, and how are you?
Thank you, I am fine. Stay well.

beats.text: LIVE EXAMPLE SLOT — add one authentic personal or community example and one cultural or register note. New isiZulu wording must be flagged for language QA before the final cut.
Now it's your turn to speak on your own — no script this time.
Greet me as if we've just met in the street. Ask how I am, answer when I ask you, and close the conversation politely.

Give a fresh variation of the lesson scenario. The learner must demonstrate: Pronounce essential sounds and open and close a culturally appropriate greeting.
Minimum evidence: understandable response, relevant approved vocabulary, one follow-up turn, and an attempt to repair if communication breaks down.
Do not provide a complete scripted answer before the attempt.
Pause and let the learner perform. Then give one specific piece of coaching.
That's the end of Lesson 1. You can now greet someone, ask how they are, answer politely, and close the conversation — with one person or a whole group.
Before the next lesson, greet someone out loud at least three times. Say it slowly, then naturally.
In Lesson 2, we'll go one step further: introducing yourself, and learning someone else's name and where they're from.
